paras: The whipping of a Black barber in Washington, Georgia, was an assault in which unnamed men took out a "negro barber" of the town, who had said he knew where Confederate gold was buried, and whipped him "nearly to death" to make him tell where it was. The Atlanta Constitution mentioned it in December 1881, in an article defending Jefferson Davis against a charge that he had misused Confederate funds.

In December 1881 an interview in which General Joseph E. Johnston suggested that Davis had misapplied about two and a half million dollars of Confederate funds set off wide press discussion. The Constitution answered that the Confederate treasure train had been robbed near Washington, in Wilkes County, Georgia, and quoted two witnesses to that effect. Its business manager, Mr. Hemphill, said that afterward there were "negroes throughout the neighborhood" holding gold from the scattered train, and many locals believed more of it lay buried nearby.

A barber of the town, described only as "a negro," had stated that he knew where the gold was buried. Men who insisted that he tell them where the gold lay took him out and whipped him nearly to death. The account gives no date beyond "a short time ago" and does not name the barber, the place, or the number of men.
No report of arrests or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

The whipping reached print only as one clause near the end of a long political article about the Confederate treasure, and no paper ran it as a separate news item. The Memphis Daily Appeal carried the Constitution's text in an Atlanta dispatch of December 21 under the headline "About that Confederate Treasure." A week later the Fairfield News and Herald of Winnsboro, South Carolina, worked the same passage into an editorial calling Johnston "billious" toward Davis.

Both papers used the incident as evidence that gold from the robbed train was believed to lie near Washington, and so as support for Davis, rather than as a crime to be condemned. Neither commented on the whipping itself or called for an investigation.

bases: Unnamed men took out a Black barber and whipped him nearly to death to force him to reveal where gold was buried; the text describes no organized band or regulating motive, so the record's "whitecapping" is not supported (A1).
The only report is the Atlanta Constitution passage reprinted in A1; A2 copies the same sentence and adds no independent information.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution
accounts.gist: A Black barber who said he knew where Confederate gold was buried near Washington was taken out and whipped nearly to death by men demanding its location.

framing.detail: Headlined "About that Confederate Treasure," the article cites the whipping only as proof that gold was believed buried near Washington, with no comment on the assault.
Folded into an editorial defending Davis against Johnston's charge; the whipping goes unremarked.
